Home » Diagnostics » Traps

Traps

Codepoints that raise the stream into the diagnostic subsystem.

The trap range 0x7FFFFFF0–0x7FFFFFFE sits at the top of the Native Space. Consuming a trap raises the current instruction stream into the diagnostic subsystem — the SuperUnicode equivalent of a hardware interrupt.

Dispatch mapping

The registry functions (sucs_bancode_to_trap() and friends) map a registry codepoint to its trap. A hard BANcode halts or rolls back; a WARNcode warns and continues; the cursor behavior follows the instruction type.

BANcode 0x0011A0xx → trap 0x7FFFFFF0+ // hard: halt/rollback
WARNcode 0x0011A8xx → warn and continue // cursor advances

System vs. App mode

Kernel Security Trap dispatch is the System mode path and is reserved for the krnl. Each of the 15 trap slots (0x7FFFFFF0–0x7FFFFFFE) governs a cluster of 128 B+ BANcodes, and the fitted damage-control handler runs in the crash context.

In App mode, fatal BANcodes never reach the trap table. The application registers its own crash handler (bancode_register_app_crash_handler()), and a fatal B+ BANcode is delivered straight to it — the app crashes on its own terms, and the krnl dispatch machinery stays untouched.

Terminal region data: sudat/control/Traps.txt and Sentinel.txt.
